newsitem.title: POLAND: Mixed feelings in East Europe greet NATO decision.
newsitem.headline: Mixed feelings in East Europe greet NATO decision.

text.p: Central and East European reaction ranged from joy through determination to outright anger on Wednesday after NATO's decision to invite only Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to begin entry talks.

"This day is among the most important in the last three centuries of Polish history because fate has not treated Poles kindly for the past 300 years" former dissident Adam Michnik wrote in the Gazeta Wyborcza from Poland.
But Bulgaria's Kontinent, lamenting the fact that NATO had not even mentioned Bulgaria as a potential member, headlined its story simply: "NATO is forgetting us."

Issuing the invitations in Madrid on Tuesday, NATO leaders also mentioned Romania and Slovenia as deserving cases when the enlargement process is renewed in 1999 and held out future hopes to the Baltic states as aspiring members.
For Poles across the political spectrum, 80 percent of whom support joining, inclusion held hopes of regional stability and security after centuries of foreign invasion.
It was also widely seen as redressing a historic wrong committed by Western allies who reluctantly left them to almost 50 years of Soviet domination at the 1945 Yalta summit.
The government, led by ex-communists, said in a statement that the decisions "constitute a closing of the Yalta era".
But Poland, keen to avoid areas of security vacuum in its region and to back its neighbours, urged NATO not to exclude any other country which wanted to enter in future.
Commentators stressed that a long road awaited Poland in meeting NATO military standards, keeping up economic growth and securing ratification by parliaments of the pact's 16 members.

Hungarian daily Magyar Hirlap wrote: "Hungary badly needs today to be finally accepted by the continent in which it has been for a thousand years. The Madrid summit made not only an invitation but a challenge - which Hungary should meet."
A sober message also came from the Czech Republic, where half of the population are unsure NATO entry is a good idea.
The largest Czech daily, Mlada Fronta Dnes, said the invitation did not mean only security guarantees but "our own greater share in the defence of world security".

Still, it quoted former prime minister Petr Pithart, a one-time dissident who is now chairman of the Czech Senate as saying: "This is a great day for Czech history, the young Czech Republic and mainly for us, the often-tested Czech people."
Meanwhile Slovak Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar, whose country was left in the cold following Western criticism of its political and economic progress, cried foul.

"It must be said that many states applied different measures in assessing eligibility for membership -- one for themselves, another for their neighbours, and another for us," Bratislava daily Sme quoted him as saying.
Romania, blocked now by the United States despite strong support from France and Italy, was determined to work hard to secure admission next time round.

"It could have been better, just as it could have been worse," President Emil Constantinescu told a television interviewer late on Tuesday. "What's important now is that all participants said they appreciated the progress made by Romania. This means we must go on."

Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, independent since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, are desperate for NATO entry for fear that Russia might turn against democracy and become hostile, although Moscow's strong opposition is a major obstacle.
Lithuania's Vytautas Landsbergis, a former dissident who is now speaker of parliament, regretted the summit declaration did not mention the three states individually. But he welcomed it.
"The declaration is a real step to the increased security of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia," he said in a statement.
Estonian daily Eesti Paevaleht also betrayed irritation.
"If expansion starts, it may continue. And NATO stuck its head in the sand like an ostrich and did not mention the three countries, but only the Baltic region," it added.
But in Madrid, Estonian President Lennart Meri said he hoped the Baltics would be considered in the next wave, having made great strides in military and economic preparations.
A Latvian diplomat said his country was satisfied with Madrid, which he said would help prospects of entering NATO.
